content: Chlamydia trachomatis is a sexually transmitted infection that can be transmitted from mother to child during childbirth. This transmission may lead to serious neonatal complications such as ophthalmia neonatorum (a form of conjunctivitis) or pneumonitis (lung inflammation) in the newborn. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of antibiotics in treating genital Chlamydia trachomatis infections during pregnancy, with a focus on reducing both neonatal and maternal morbidity. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register, with the initial search completed in September 2006. An updated search was performed on January 3, 2012, which identified one additional trial report awaiting classification. The review included randomized controlled trials that compared any antibiotic regimen to either a placebo, no treatment, or alternative antibiotic regimens in pregnant women diagnosed with genital Chlamydia trachomatis infection. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the included trials and extracted relevant data. When necessary, the authors of the studies were contacted to obtain additional information. A total of 11 trials were included in the review, and the overall quality of the trials was deemed to be good. The findings indicated that amoxicillin was as effective as erythromycin in achieving microbiological cure, with an odds ratio of 0.54 (95% confidence interval: 0.28 to 1.02). Furthermore, amoxicillin was better tolerated by patients compared to erythromycin, with an odds ratio of 0.16 (95% confidence interval: 0.09 to 0.30). Clindamycin and azithromycin also appeared to be effective treatment options, although the number of participants in the trials evaluating these antibiotics was relatively small. The authors concluded that amoxicillin is a suitable alternative to erythromycin for the treatment of genital Chlamydia trachomatis infections during pregnancy. Clindamycin and azithromycin may also be considered as treatment options, particularly in cases where erythromycin and amoxicillin are contraindicated or poorly tolerated. It is important to note that seven studies awaiting classification at the time of this review may influence the conclusions once they are fully assessed.
